2870:
Clamant means urgently and insistently demanding attention — so loud, pressing, or forceful that it simply cannot be ignored.

Think of it this way: when something is clamant, it is essentially "screaming to be noticed." It could be a literal voice crying out loudly, or more commonly, a problem, need, or situation that is so urgent and pressing that it demands an immediate response.

Clamant carries two closely related senses, and understanding both will give you the full picture:

1. Literally loud and crying out
At its most direct, clamant describes something or someone making a loud, insistent outcry — raising their voice urgently and forcefully.

"The clamant crowd refused to be silenced until the governor appeared."

Here, the crowd is not just noisy — they are insistently and urgently demanding to be heard.

2. Figuratively urgent and pressing
This is the far more common usage in modern writing. Here, clamant describes a need, problem, or issue that is so urgent it feels like it is crying out to be addressed — even if no actual sound is involved.

"There is a clamant need for clean drinking water in the region."
"The report highlighted several clamant issues that the government had long neglected."

In this sense, the word doesn't describe noise at all. It describes urgency — the kind of urgency that demands you stop everything else and pay attention right now.
What Makes It Different from Similar Words

You might wonder: why not just say urgent, pressing, or desperate? These words are close, but clamant carries something extra — a sense of forceful insistence, almost as if the thing itself is raising its voice and refusing to be pushed aside or delayed. It is not merely important; it is actively, loudly demanding a response.

Compare:

  • "An urgent problem" — needs to be addressed soon.
  • "A pressing problem" — weighing heavily, pushing for action.
  • "A clamant problem" — so urgent and insistent that it feels like it is shouting at you.

The emotional intensity in clamant is noticeably stronger.

This is a formal and literary word. You will most often find it in:

  • Formal essays and academic writing
  • Political or social commentary
  • Older or classic literature
  • Formal speeches and journalism

You would not say "My clamant stomach needs lunch" in everyday conversation. Instead, you might write: "The clamant demands of the opposition could no longer be dismissed by the ruling party."

Using clamant in casual conversation would sound unusual or overly dramatic. Save it for formal or serious contexts.

Think of the word clamor — a loud, demanding noise. Clamant is the adjective form of that same energy. Something clamant has the quality of clamoring — of being so loud and insistent, whether literally or figuratively, that it forces you to respond.

Clamant describes something — a need, problem, voice, or situation — that is so urgently and insistently demanding that it cannot reasonably be ignored, as if it were crying out at full volume for an immediate response.
2871:
To clamber means to climb something in a clumsy, effortful way — using both your hands and your feet (or your whole body) to pull yourself up, over, or through something difficult.

It is not smooth. It is not graceful. It is the kind of climbing where you are almost struggling, grabbing whatever you can, pushing with your legs, pulling with your arms, and working hard just to get to where you want to go.

She clambered up the rocky hillside.

You can immediately picture someone not walking up neatly, but grabbing rocks with their hands, finding footholds, maybe slipping a little — working their way up with effort.
The Two Things That Make "Clamber" Unique

Almost every other word in English for climbing misses one or both of these two qualities that "clamber" always carries:

1. It involves the whole body — especially the hands

Regular climbing can mean many things. You climb stairs, for instance, using only your legs, walking upright, perfectly elegantly. But you would never say you clambered up the stairs unless you were literally on your hands and knees struggling up them. Clambering almost always involves the hands gripping, grabbing, and helping the body move. You are not walking — you are hauling yourself somewhere using your limbs together.

2. It always involves difficulty and effort

This is the heart of the word. Clamber is never effortless. The surface is awkward, the path is uneven, the obstacle is challenging — and so your body responds by working harder, becoming less elegant, and using every limb available. The difficulty is baked into the word itself. If it were easy, you would just walk or climb. When you clamber, something is demanding more from you.

"Clamber" carries a strong visual sense of ungainliness — meaning it is not a pretty sight. When someone clambers, they may look a little undignified. Think of a person trying to get out of a low, deep sofa, or a child hauling themselves over a garden wall. There is something almost comical or relatable about it. It is very human and very real.

This is an important part of the word's personality. Writers often choose "clamber" precisely because they want you to picture that slightly awkward, full-body effort — not a clean, athletic move, but a genuine physical struggle.
Direction: Which Way Do You Clamber?

Most of the time, clambering goes upward or over something:

  • Clamber up a tree, a cliff, a wall, a slope
  • Clamber over a fence, a boulder, rubble, a pile of objects
  • Clamber out of a tight or awkward space (like the back seat of a car, or a ditch)
  • Clamber through a gap or a difficult narrow passage

You would almost never use "clamber" for moving on a flat, easy surface. The word needs an obstacle, a height, or a challenge to justify itself.

Here are sentences that show the word at work. Notice how each one paints a clear picture of struggle and full-body effort:

  • The children clambered over the fallen tree blocking the path.

(They didn't step over it neatly — they grabbed it, swung their legs over, heaved themselves across.)

  • He clambered up onto the roof to fix the broken tile.

(Not a smooth, easy climb — a real effort involving hands, feet, and body.)

  • She clambered out of the wrecked car as fast as she could.

(The car was damaged and awkward to exit — it took real physical maneuvering.)

  • The rescue team clambered through the rubble looking for survivors.

(Difficult, unstable ground; no graceful walking possible.)

  • The toddler clambered up onto the sofa with great determination.

(The sofa was too tall and high for the child to simply step up — full-body effort required.)

You may come across words that seem close to "clamber." Here is how to keep them straight:

Climb — The broad, neutral word. Can be easy or hard, graceful or clumsy. Doesn't tell you much about how it's done. You climb stairs effortlessly. You would never clamber up stairs unless something went wrong.

Scramble — Similar to clamber in that it uses hands and feet and implies difficulty, but scramble adds a layer of speed and urgency — often a sense of panic or haste. You scramble when you are in a rush or a desperate situation. Clambering is slower and more labored; scrambling is frantic.

Crawl — Moving on hands and knees on a flat surface, horizontally, low to the ground. No upward movement implied. Clamber is distinctly about going up or over, not just along the ground.

Scale — To scale something (a wall, a mountain) means to climb it, but this word sounds more formal and impressive — like an achievement. Scaling has a sense of accomplishment and height. Clambering sounds more effortful and less elegant.
A Quick Test to Know When to Use "Clamber"

Ask yourself three questions:

  1. Is the person using their hands and feet together to move? ✓
  2. Is there real effort and difficulty involved? ✓
  3. Are they going upward, over, or out of something awkward? ✓

If all three answers are yes — clamber is your word.
To clamber is to climb something difficult in a clumsy, full-body way — using your hands and feet together, with clear effort and without grace.
2872: Something is clammy when it feels unpleasantly damp, cold, and slightly sticky all at once. It is not just wet. It is not just cold. It has a specific, uncomfortable combination of all three — and that combined feeling is what "clammy" captures.

Imagine touching a surface and feeling:

  • a light moisture (not dripping, but not dry either)
  • a coolness (or at least not warm)
  • a subtle stickiness, as if it slightly clings to your fingers

That is clammy. The word almost always carries a sense of discomfort — it describes a feeling that most people find unpleasant or unsettling.
Where you will most often encounter it: skin

The single most common use of "clammy" is to describe human skin, especially the hands.

When a person is nervous, frightened, ill, in shock, or very anxious, their body often produces a kind of cool, sticky sweat. The skin does not feel warm and flushed — it feels cold and slightly wet, almost like touching the outside of a glass of cold water that has some condensation on it.

"Before the job interview, her palms were clammy."
"The doctor noticed that the patient's skin was clammy — a sign something was wrong."
"He reached out for a handshake, but his hand was cold and clammy."

This is the classic image: clammy skin = a sign of fear, stress, sickness, or shock.
The important difference from just "sweaty" or "wet"

Many learners confuse clammy with simply being sweaty or wet. Here is the key distinction:

  • Sweaty can be warm — like after exercise, when your skin is hot and drenched. That is not clammy.
  • Clammy leans cold. It is the uncomfortable, cool moisture — not the hot flush of effort.

Clammy sweat feels wrong in a particular way. It is the sweat of fear, not of hard work.
Other things that can be clammy

While skin is the most common use, "clammy" can describe other things too:

The air or atmosphere:
A damp, cold, heavy air — like the air inside an old cave, a cellar, or a foggy morning by a river — can feel clammy. It clings to you. It is not refreshing; it feels oppressive and wet.

"The air in the basement was clammy and cold."
"She stepped outside into the clammy morning fog."

Surfaces:
A cold, damp wall (like in an old building or underground tunnel), a wet towel left out overnight, or a stone floor can feel clammy when you touch it.

"The walls of the dungeon were clammy with moisture."
The tone and feeling the word carries

"Clammy" is almost never a neutral word. It almost always signals something negative — discomfort, illness, fear, decay, or dread. Writers use it deliberately to make a scene feel uneasy or wrong.

In literature and everyday speech, it often appears in contexts of:

  • Fear or horror — "a clammy feeling crept over him"
  • Illness — "the fever broke and left her clammy and exhausted"
  • Unpleasant environments — "the clammy darkness of the tunnel"
A quick mental image to anchor it

Think of shaking hands with someone who is terrified. Their hand is cool, slightly wet, and just a little sticky — not warm, not dripping, but deeply uncomfortable to touch. That handshake is the definition of clammy.

Clammy means unpleasantly cold, damp, and slightly sticky — most often used to describe skin during fear, illness, or shock, but also used for cold, damp air or surfaces — and it almost always suggests discomfort or something being wrong.
2873:
Clamorous describes something or someone that is loud, noisy, and impossible to ignore — but not just "loud" in a simple way. The word carries a specific flavor: it suggests noise or demands that are urgent, insistent, and overwhelming, often coming from multiple directions at once, like a storm of sound or pressure crashing into you.

If "loud" is just about volume, think of clamorous as volume + urgency + chaos. It's the kind of noise or demand that feels like it's grabbing you by the collar and refusing to let go.

Clamorous works in two closely related ways:

1. Describing Loud, Chaotic Sounds or Environments

When used this way, it describes a scene or a sound that is so loud and overwhelming that it feels almost out of control — a jumble of noise hitting you all at once.

The school cafeteria was clamorous at lunchtime, with hundreds of children shouting, laughing, and scraping chairs all at once.

The market was clamorous — vendors yelling prices, music blaring, and customers arguing in every corner.

Notice: it's not the quiet hum of a library or even the steady roar of a waterfall (which is loud but orderly). Clamorous implies messy, layered, demanding noise — the kind that is hard to think through.

2. Describing People or Groups Who Are Loudly and Persistently Demanding Something

This is perhaps the more powerful and more commonly used sense. Here, clamorous describes people who are making a loud, insistent, and urgent demand — they aren't politely asking; they are pressing hard, raising their voices, and refusing to be ignored.

The workers were clamorous in their demand for fair wages, chanting and protesting outside the factory gates for days.

The crowd grew clamorous, shouting for the manager to come and explain what had happened.

The key idea here is that clamorous people or groups are not being subtle. They want something, they want it now, and they are making absolutely sure everyone around them knows it.

Clamorous is not a neutral word. It almost always carries a slightly negative or at least overwhelming tone. When you call something clamorous, you're usually suggesting it's:

  • Excessive — the noise or the demands feel like too much
  • Hard to control or silence — it has a sense of things spilling over
  • Disruptive — it interrupts, overwhelms, or unsettles

You would rarely call a beautiful symphony clamorous, even if it's loud — because a symphony is organized and controlled. Clamorous implies something more raw and unruly.
What Clamorous Is Not — Sharpening the Definition

Because words are best understood by their edges, here's what separates clamorous from similar words:

  • Loud — Just means high in volume. A single guitar chord can be loud. Clamorous implies urgency and chaos on top of volume.
  • Noisy — General and informal. "My neighbors are noisy." Clamorous is stronger, more vivid, and more literary.
  • Boisterous — Describes lively, energetic, and cheerful noisiness (like kids playing). Clamorous has a harder, more pressured edge — it's less playful.
  • Vociferous — The closest relative. Vociferous also describes loud, insistent people — but vociferous focuses more on the speaking/shouting itself, while clamorous captures the overall atmosphere of overwhelming noise and demand. A crowd can be clamorous; a single outspoken critic is more often vociferous.
Who or What Can Be Clamorous?

The word is flexible. All of these work naturally:

  • A crowd can be clamorous (noisy and demanding)
  • A group of protesters can be clamorous (loudly insisting on change)
  • A marketplace or street can be clamorous (overwhelmingly loud)
  • Demands or calls can be clamorous (urgent and impossible to ignore)
  • Children can be clamorous (loud and relentlessly demanding attention)

To remember this word instantly, picture a large, angry crowd — dozens of people all shouting at the same time, demanding the same thing, and refusing to lower their voices until someone listens. That crowd is clamorous. The noise they make is clamorous. The demands they are making are clamorous.

Whenever you see or feel something loud, urgent, chaotic, and insistent — that's your word.
2874:
Imagine you're watching a protest outside a government building. Hundreds of people are shouting, chanting, and demanding change — all at the same time. The air is thick with overlapping voices, rising and falling but never stopping. That overwhelming wall of sound and collective demand is a clamour.

"Clamour" means a loud, sustained, and confused noise produced by many people together, usually driven by strong emotion — and/or a strong, widespread demand or protest from a large group.
The Two Sides of the Word

"Clamour" works on two levels, and understanding both is key.

1. The Physical/Sound Sense

This is the most literal sense: a very loud, continuous noise made by many voices or sounds mixed together. The important word here is many — one person shouting is not a clamour. It takes a crowd, a mob, a marketplace, or a stadium full of people to create one. The noise isn't clean or organised — it's messy, overlapping, and overwhelming.

The clamour of the marketplace made it impossible to hear your own thoughts.

As the fire alarm went off, a clamour broke out in the hallways.

The clamour of the crowd in the stadium was deafening.

2. The Figurative/Demand Sense

This is an extension of the first: a loud, insistent, collective demand or protest. Here, "clamour" isn't just about raw noise — it's about the force and persistence of people collectively calling for something. Even in writing, when journalists say "there was a clamour for justice," they mean a strong, sustained, widespread call from many people — not a polite request.

There was a growing clamour for the president's resignation.

The clamour for better wages finally forced the company to negotiate.

Despite the clamour of public opinion, the government refused to act.

What makes a sound or a demand a clamour — and not just any noise or request? Four things must be present:

1. Loudness — A clamour is never quiet or subtle. It is inherently loud and impossible to ignore.

2. Many sources — It always comes from multiple people or things at once. One voice cannot produce a clamour.

3. Confusion and overlap — The sounds or voices in a clamour are tangled together. It is not an organised, structured sound — it is a mix.

4. Strong emotion and persistence — A clamour is not a passing moment. It is sustained and charged with emotion — anger, excitement, grief, outrage, protest, or urgency.

Remove any one of these qualities and you might have noise, or a request, or a shout — but you don't quite have a clamour.
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words often get confused with "clamour," but each has a different flavour:

  • Din — A continuous, loud, irritating noise, but it doesn't necessarily come from people and doesn't carry the sense of emotional demand. A factory machine makes a din; a crowd makes a clamour.
  • Uproar — This emphasises disorder and chaos more than sound itself. An uproar is a situation; a clamour is a sound/voice.
  • Outcry — An outcry is a strong public protest or reaction, but it doesn't have to be physically loud. A clamour always feels louder and more visceral.
  • Hubbub — A low-level, confused mixture of sounds or activity. A hubbub is mild; a clamour is intense.
  • Tumult — This emphasises physical disorder and commotion. A tumult may be noisy, but "clamour" focuses specifically on the vocal and auditory dimension.
  • Racket — Simply an unpleasant loud noise, with no emotional or collective dimension. Children playing noisily make a racket; protesters at a parliament make a clamour.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

"Clamour" carries a certain weight and drama. When a writer uses it, they are signalling that what is happening is not ordinary noise — it is urgent, collective, emotionally raw, and hard to ignore. It has a slightly formal or literary tone, which is why you'll see it more in books, journalism, and formal writing than in casual conversation.

It always implies that something important is at stake — people don't clamour about trivial things. They clamour when they feel strongly, when they are unheard, when they are demanding change or expressing powerful emotion.

Certain words naturally appear alongside "clamour" in English:

  • A clamour for something — a clamour for reform / justice / attention / change (a collective demand)
  • A clamour of something — a clamour of voices / bells / protest (describing what makes up the noise)
  • Raise a clamour — to create or cause a clamour
  • A growing clamour — a demand that is increasing in strength over time
  • Above the clamour — used to describe something heard or noticed despite the noise
A Final Image to Lock It In

Picture a medieval king walking into his court after making a deeply unpopular decision. Instantly, every noble, advisor, and soldier in the room erupts — all shouting, arguing, and demanding he reconsider. The voices crash into each other. The room fills with an almost physical force of sound and collective anger. Nobody can be heard individually, but together their voices form one overwhelming force.

That is clamour — many voices, loud and persistent, fused together by shared emotion into something bigger than any one of them.
2875:
To clamp down on something means to take strong, strict action to stop, control, or limit something — especially something that is considered harmful, illegal, or problematic.

Think of it simply as: "to get tough on something."
Understanding It Through the Literal Image

The word clamp refers to a physical tool — a device that grips two things tightly together so that nothing can move, slip, or escape. Imagine a carpenter using a metal clamp to hold two pieces of wood firmly in place. The clamp presses down hard and allows no movement.

Now take that image and use it as a metaphor. When an authority "clamps down on" something, they are essentially gripping it tightly to make sure it stops happening or spreading. The idea is one of force, pressure, and control.
Who Uses This Idiom?

This idiom almost always involves a person or body in authority, such as:

  • A government
  • The police
  • A school or university
  • A company's management
  • A regulatory body or organization

Regular individuals rarely "clamp down" on things. It is the language of power and enforcement.
What Gets "Clamped Down On"?

The thing being clamped down on is always something negative or unwanted — something that needs to be stopped or brought under control. Examples include:

  • Crime
  • Corruption
  • Illegal activity
  • A bad habit or behaviour
  • Rule-breaking
  • Excessive spending

You would never say someone "clamped down on" something good or desirable. The idiom always carries the idea of suppressing something undesirable.
Important Nuance: A Sudden Tightening of Control

Here is a subtle but important point: clamp down on usually implies that control is being increased — meaning the authority is becoming stricter than before. It suggests that the problem existed for a while without being fully controlled, and now someone has decided: "Enough. We're taking serious action."

So it carries a sense of a decisive shift — from being lenient or relaxed to being firm and strict.
Examples in Sentences

These examples will show you how naturally the idiom is used:

  • "The government decided to clamp down on tax fraud after billions of dollars went missing."

(The government took strict action to stop people from avoiding taxes.)

  • "Police are clamping down on speeding in residential areas."

(Police are enforcing the rules more strictly and punishing speeding more aggressively.)

  • "The school clamped down on the use of mobile phones during class."

(The school introduced stricter rules to stop students from using phones in lessons.)

  • "After the data breach, the company clamped down on who could access sensitive files."

(The company tightened security and restricted access more severely than before.)

  • "The new mayor promised to clamp down on corruption in local government."

(The mayor promised to take strong action to eliminate corruption.)
Grammar: How to Use It Correctly

Clamp down on is a phrasal verb. Here is how it works grammatically:

Structure: Subject + clamp(s)/clamped + down + on + object

  • Present tense: "The authorities clamp down on illegal dumping every summer."
  • Past tense: "The authorities clamped down on illegal dumping last year."
  • Present continuous: "The authorities are clamping down on illegal dumping right now."

Important: The three words — clamp, down, and on — must always stay together. You cannot separate them. You cannot say "clamp on" or "clamp down" without "on" and expect the same meaning.
The Noun Form: "A Clampdown"

This idiom also has a noun form: clampdown (written as one word).

  • "There has been a massive clampdown on drug trafficking in the region."
  • "The new clampdown on noise pollution came after years of complaints."

The noun form means the action or period of strict enforcement itself.
Synonyms and Related Expressions

These expressions are similar in meaning and can often be used in the same context:

  • Crack down on — very close in meaning; perhaps the most common synonym
  • Stamp out — suggests eliminating something completely (e.g., "stamp out corruption")
  • Tighten control over — more formal and literal
  • Put a stop to — simpler and more direct
  • Come down hard on — emphasises the harshness of the punishment or response
How to Remember It Forever

Picture this scene in your mind:

A giant metal clamp comes down from the sky and squeezes something tightly — a crime, a bad habit, a problem — until it cannot breathe or move. It is trapped and stopped.

That is exactly what "clamp down on" means. Someone powerful brings down a force so strong that a problem has no room left to continue.
Quick Summary

ElementDetail
  • Meaning: To take strong, strict action to stop or control something undesirable.
  • Who does it: An authority (government, police, school, company).
  • What is clamped down on: Something negative — crime, bad behaviour, illegal activity.
  • Key nuance: It suggests a tightening of control — becoming stricter than before.
  • Noun form: A clampdown.
  • Closest synonym: Crack down on.
2876: A clan is a large group of people who are all connected to each other through a shared ancestor — a common person in the distant past from whom everyone in the group descends. Think of it as a very large, extended family tree where all the branches ultimately grow from the same root.

Imagine your grandfather had four children. Those four children each had their own children, who had more children, and so on for many generations. After several hundred years, there would be hundreds or even thousands of people who all trace their bloodline back to that one grandfather. That entire network of people, united by that shared bloodline and the identity that comes with it, is what we call a clan.

The key ingredients are:

  • Shared ancestry — All members (or at least most of them) believe they descend from one common ancestor, even if that ancestor lived so long ago that no living member ever met them.
  • A collective identity — A clan usually has a name, often a family name or the name of their founding ancestor. Members identify themselves as part of that clan. It becomes part of who they are.
  • Strong loyalty and solidarity — Members of a clan feel a deep sense of belonging to one another. They are expected to support, protect, and stand by each other — especially against outsiders.
  • A sense of shared history and tradition — Clans carry stories, customs, and sometimes symbols (like a flag, an emblem, or a specific pattern of clothing) that belong to their group and no one else.
How a Clan is Different from a "Family" and a "Tribe"

These three words are often confused, so it helps to see how they compare.

Family refers to the smaller, more immediate group — your parents, siblings, grandparents, aunts, uncles, cousins. It's the people you personally know and are directly related to. A family fits around a dinner table (or not too far beyond it).

Clan is bigger. It is made up of many families who all share the same distant ancestor. You may not personally know every member of your clan, but you share a name, a bloodline, and a collective identity with all of them. It is a community built on kinship.

Tribe is usually even bigger than a clan. A tribe can be a collection of several clans, or a broader group of people united not just by blood but also by shared language, land, culture, and way of life.

So the scale goes roughly: family → clan → tribe.

Scottish clans are perhaps the most well-known example in the world. Scotland has hundreds of historical clans — Clan MacDonald, Clan Campbell, Clan MacGregor, and many others. Each clan had its own territory, its own chief (a leader who headed the clan), and its own symbol called a tartan (a specific pattern of colors woven into fabric). If you belonged to Clan MacDonald, you owed loyalty to the MacDonald chief, and other MacDonalds were your people. Rivalries and alliances between clans shaped Scottish history for centuries.

Japanese clans also played a huge role in history. Powerful clans like the Fujiwara, the Minamoto, and the Taira competed for political power and control of the country for centuries. The samurai class was deeply organized around clan loyalty.

Native American cultures have clans too, though they work somewhat differently. In many Native American nations, clans are organized around animals or natural symbols (like the Bear Clan or the Turtle Clan), and they serve important social functions — such as deciding who can marry whom (members of the same clan are often not allowed to marry each other).

Arabic and many African cultures have deeply rooted clan systems as well, where a person's clan membership determines their social status, their alliances, and sometimes their obligations under customary law.
The Chief: The Head of a Clan

Clans are typically led by someone called a chief (or an equivalent title in different cultures). The chief is usually the eldest or most respected member of the founding family's direct line. The chief makes decisions for the clan, settles internal disputes, represents the clan to outsiders, and is owed loyalty and obedience by the clan's members in return for protection and leadership.

A clan is not just a biological fact — it is a social and emotional reality. Being part of a clan means:

  • You have an identity that is bigger than yourself. You are not just an individual; you are a MacDonald, a Fujiwara, a member of the Bear Clan.
  • You have people who will stand by you. In societies and historical periods where there was no police, no courts, and no government to protect individuals, your clan was your protection. If someone harmed you, your clan would respond.
  • You have obligations. The loyalty works both ways. You are expected to help, defend, and honor your clan members, just as they would do for you.
  • You inherit a reputation. The honor or shame of a clan is shared by all its members, which makes reputation deeply important in clan-based societies.

In modern, everyday English — especially in informal speech — "clan" is also used loosely and warmly to refer to any close-knit group of people, not necessarily related by blood. For example:

  • "The whole clan is coming over for the holidays" — meaning the entire extended family.
  • "He brought his clan with him" — meaning his tight group of friends or associates.

In this casual sense, "clan" carries a tone of warmth and togetherness. It suggests a group that is closely bonded, loyal to each other, and operates somewhat as a unit.

A clan is a large group of people bound together by descent from a common ancestor, a shared name and identity, and deep mutual loyalty. It is bigger than a family but often smaller than a tribe. Clans are found across nearly every human culture and have historically been one of the most fundamental ways human beings organize themselves socially. Even in the modern world, the word survives — both in its precise historical sense and as a warm, informal way to describe any tightly bonded group of people.
2877:
Clandestine means done in secret — especially because it is forbidden, disapproved of, or would cause serious trouble if discovered.

When something is clandestine, it is not just private. It is deliberately hidden from specific people — usually those in authority, or those who would stop it from happening.
The Key Idea: Hiding Because You Have To

This is the soul of the word. Think of it this way:

  • A surprise birthday party is secret, but it is not clandestine. Nobody is trying to hide wrongdoing. There is no risk, no danger, no rule being broken.
  • A spy meeting a foreign agent in a basement at midnight — that is clandestine. It is hidden because exposure would mean arrest, danger, or failure of a mission.

The difference is motivation for secrecy. Clandestine secrecy always carries the weight of "we cannot let the wrong people find out."

Clandestine is not a neutral word. It carries a strong atmosphere of:

  • Stealth — careful, calculated hiding
  • Risk — there are real consequences if discovered
  • Intentionality — nothing about it is accidentally secret; the secrecy is planned

When you read or hear the word "clandestine," you should immediately feel a sense of underground activity — something happening in the shadows, away from watchful eyes.

Clandestine is used to describe activities, operations, meetings, organizations, or relationships — things that involve ongoing action or interaction.

Here are strong, natural examples of how it is used:

  • A clandestine operation — a secret military or spy mission that the public or the enemy must never know about.
  • A clandestine meeting — two people meeting in secret because the meeting itself is forbidden or dangerous.
  • A clandestine affair — a romantic relationship hidden from others (usually a spouse or family).
  • A clandestine organization — a group that operates in secret because its goals are illegal or opposed by the government.
  • A clandestine radio station — a station broadcasting illegally or against the will of authorities.

This is important for precision:

  • It does not simply mean "private." Your diary is private, not clandestine.
  • It does not mean "quiet" or "low-key." A quiet evening at home is not clandestine.
  • It does not always mean illegal — but it always implies that someone in power would disapprove or intervene if they knew.

The word requires the element of hiding something from someone who matters — an authority, a government, a spouse, a rival, etc.
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words are close to clandestine, but each has its own shade of meaning:

Secret — the broadest word. Anything not publicly known. It carries no specific tone of danger or wrongdoing. Clandestine is a stronger, more loaded form of secret.

Covert — very close to clandestine, and often used interchangeably in the context of intelligence or military work. However, "covert" tends to be more technical and neutral (a covert operation is simply a hidden one). "Clandestine" carries more of a forbidden or illicit flavor.

Undercover — specifically describes a person pretending to be someone else to gather information (an undercover detective). Clandestine describes the nature of an activity, not a disguise.

Surreptitious — describes an action done quickly and sneakily, often in the moment (a surreptitious glance). Clandestine describes something more sustained and organized over time.

Furtive — describes behavior — the nervous, shifty way a person acts when hiding something (a furtive look over the shoulder). Clandestine describes the activity itself, not the body language around it.

To place this word on a scale of secrecy:

Private → Secret → Clandestine → Covert

Private and secret are relatively mild. Clandestine implies active concealment with stakes. Covert sits alongside clandestine but leans more toward formal, professional intelligence contexts.
Sentences That Show the Word in Full Colour

1. The two rebels held a clandestine meeting in an abandoned warehouse, knowing that discovery would mean immediate arrest.
  2. For years, the government ran a clandestine surveillance program that even most lawmakers were unaware of.
  3. Their clandestine relationship lasted three years before it was finally exposed.
  4. The journalist had spent months uncovering evidence of clandestine financial dealings between the corporation and corrupt officials.
  5. The resistance movement operated through a network of clandestine cells, each knowing as little about the others as possible.

Notice in every sentence: there is intentional hiding, there are real consequences for being found out, and there is always someone who must not know.
One-Line Summary to Lock It In

Clandestine = secretly done, because exposure would bring serious consequences — whether from authority, law, or those who hold power over the situation.

If you ever feel unsure whether to use it, ask yourself: "Is this being hidden because someone powerful would stop it or punish it?" If yes — clandestine fits perfectly.
2878: Clangor means a loud, harsh, metallic ringing or banging sound — especially one that is continuous, repeated, or fills the air. It is not just any loud noise. It is specifically the kind of sound made by large metal objects striking each other or vibrating forcefully. Think of enormous iron bells being struck hard, swords clashing in battle, hammers pounding an anvil, or heavy chains dragging across stone. That overwhelming, resonant, metallic noise — that is clangor.
What makes a sound "clangor" and not just "noise"?

Three qualities define it:

  • It is metallic. It comes from metal, or at least sounds like it does — hard, resonant, ring-like.
  • It is loud and forceful. It is not a gentle chime or a soft ring. It has weight and impact.
  • It is sustained or repeated. A single brief clang is just a "clang." When that sound keeps going, overlaps, or echoes and fills the air around you, it becomes clangor.

The word captures the sense of sound that overwhelms the air — you don't just hear it, you feel it around you.

• A fire truck's bell ringing continuously as it rushes through the streets — that relentless metallic ringing is clangor.
  • A medieval blacksmith's workshop with hammers constantly striking iron — the collective noise filling the smithy is clangor.
  • Giant cathedral bells all ringing together, their sounds colliding and filling the sky — clangor.
  • Metal scaffolding pipes falling and bouncing on a construction site — clangor.
  • Soldiers' armor and weapons clashing in a chaotic battle scene — clangor.

• "The clangor of the factory bells announced the end of the shift."
  • "She could not sleep through the clangor of the construction work outside her window."
  • "The battlefield rang with the clangor of steel on steel."
  • "A sudden clangor of church bells woke the entire village."

Writers sometimes use clangor beyond literal metallic sounds. It can describe any overwhelming, harsh, jarring commotion — like a verbal argument that is loud, discordant, and impossible to ignore.

  • "The clangor of political debate filled every newspaper."

Here, it is used as a metaphor: ideas and voices clashing loudly, just like metal on metal. This figurative use keeps the core idea intact — something loud, forceful, and hard to tune out.

Clangor almost always carries a sense of harshness, urgency, or chaos. It is not the pleasant sound of wind chimes or a soft bell. When a writer chooses this word, they want you to feel assaulted by sound — overwhelmed, perhaps unsettled. It has a dramatic, weighty quality.

This is why you encounter it more often in literature, poetry, and formal writing than in everyday speech. When a writer wants to make you feel the noise rather than just know about it, they reach for clangor.

• Clangorous (adjective): describes something that produces clangor. "The clangorous bells."
  • Clamorously / Clang: clang is a single sharp metallic sound; clangor is the sustained, ongoing version of that.
  • Clangour: the British English spelling of the exact same word. Same meaning, different spelling.
How it differs from similar words

• Clang — a single, sharp metallic sound. One hit. Clangor is many, or one sustained.
  • Din — any kind of prolonged loud noise (not necessarily metallic). Clangor is specifically metallic and resonant.
  • Clamor — loud noise or shouting, often from a crowd of people. Clangor is the metallic version of this.
  • Racket — informal word for any annoying loud noise. Clangor is more specific, more literary, and more metallic.
  • Clatter — lighter, faster, more chaotic sound (like dishes falling). Clangor is heavier and more resonant.
Clangor is the loud, harsh, resonant metallic noise — the kind that fills the air and keeps going — like great bells, clashing swords, or hammering iron.
2879: Clap means to strike two flat surfaces — most often your two palms — together sharply to produce a sound. That sharp, quick sound is central to almost everything this word means.

1. To Strike Your Palms Together (The Most Common Meaning)

This is what people do when they applaud — they bring both hands together quickly and repeatedly to make a sound. This is done to show approval, appreciation, enthusiasm, or celebration.

  • The crowd clapped loudly when the singer finished the song.
  • Everyone clapped for the children's performance.
  • She clapped in delight when she heard the good news.

You can clap once, or you can clap repeatedly. Clapping repeatedly is the act of applauding. When a whole group of people clap together like this, it is called applause, but the action each person does is "clapping."

You can also clap your hands together once — sharply — to get people's attention or to signal something:

  • The teacher clapped her hands to silence the class.
  • He clapped his hands once to call the dog.

2. To Strike One Thing Against Another

"Clap" also means to strike two hard, flat objects together to make a sharp noise. It doesn't have to be your palms — it can be any two surfaces.

  • He clapped two wooden boards together to make a loud crack.
  • She clapped the erasers together to clean the chalk dust off them.

The key feeling here is that the action is quick and produces a distinct, sharp sound.

3. To Pat or Slap Someone Lightly (Usually in a Friendly Way)

When you "clap" someone on the back or shoulder, you give them a firm but friendly pat — usually to congratulate them, encourage them, or show warmth.

  • His coach clapped him on the back and said, "Well done!"
  • She clapped her friend on the shoulder with a big smile.

This is always a single, solid contact — not a repeated striking. It conveys friendliness, pride, or encouragement. Strangers don't generally clap each other on the back; it implies closeness or familiarity.

4. To Put Something Somewhere Quickly and Firmly

"Clap" can mean to place or put something somewhere in a sudden, sharp, decisive way. The action is fast and deliberate — there's a sense of immediacy to it.

  • He clapped his hand over his mouth in shock.
  • She clapped a hat on her head and rushed out the door.
  • The officer clapped handcuffs on the suspect.

Notice how in all of these, the action is quick — it happens in an instant. This use of "clap" suggests speed and decisiveness. It isn't slow or gradual; it's sudden.

A related use, now old-fashioned but worth knowing because it appears in literature: to put someone in prison quickly and without delay — "They clapped him in jail."

5. When a Bird Claps Its Wings

Birds "clap" their wings when they beat them together — usually just above or below the body — producing a snapping or slapping sound. Some birds, like pigeons and certain doves, do this deliberately as part of a display.

  • The pigeon clapped its wings as it took off.

Across all its meanings, "clap" carries a feeling of quickness, sharpness, and decisiveness. Whatever is being clapped — hands, boards, a hand over a mouth, a hat on a head — it happens fast and produces either a sound or a firm effect.

It is also generally a positive or neutral word. Clapping for someone is an act of praise. Clapping someone on the back is warm and friendly. Even "clap your eyes on" (see below) is just casual and friendly in tone.

Clap eyes on (mainly British and Irish English, informal)
This means to see someone or something, often for the first time, or after a long time. It suggests the moment your eyes land on a person or thing.

  • I haven't clapped eyes on him in years.
  • The moment she clapped eyes on that puppy, she wanted to take it home.

Clap out (to clap a rhythm)
To produce a rhythm by clapping:

  • The children clapped out the beat of the song.

Clap back (informal, modern)
To respond sharply or wittily to a criticism or insult:

  • She clapped back at the negative comment with a clever reply.

This is used heavily in social media contexts. It implies a quick, confident counter-response.

• Slap — also a sharp contact, but usually harder and often aggressive or unpleasant; you slap someone in anger. Clapping someone on the back is friendly; slapping them is not.
  • Pat — softer and gentler than clap; you pat a dog or pat a child's head. Clapping is firmer and louder.
  • Applaud — specifically means to clap for approval or praise; "clap" is the action, "applaud" is slightly more formal and always means appreciation.
  • Smack — a single, usually hard and loud strike; more forceful and often negative compared to clap.

1. To bring your palms sharply together, once or repeatedly — to applaud or to signal something.
  2. To strike two flat objects together to make a sharp sound.
  3. To pat someone firmly and briefly on the back or shoulder as a friendly gesture.
  4. To put or place something somewhere quickly and decisively.
  5. (Of birds) to beat the wings together, producing a snapping sound.

And as a set phrase: clap eyes on = to see someone/something.
